page_hint: Ch 1, Attention section, three-row taxonomy table, 'Reduced-width per-token' row, Bytes/token column
quoted_clause: MLA ~50–60× less for DeepSeek-class geometry, [DERIVED]
observed: The claim of ~50–60× KV-cache reduction for MLA versus full MHA is marked [DERIVED] but no derivation is shown in this chapter and no cross-reference indicates where the derivation appears.
evidence: Independent rederivation for DeepSeek V2/V3 geometry (61 layers, 128 heads, d_head=128, compressed latent d_c=512): if only the compressed latent c_KV (512 dims/layer/token) is physically cached, MHA KV = 2×128×128 = 32,768 dims/layer/token, giving 32,768/512 = 64× reduction — outside the stated 50–60× range. If c_KV plus decoupled keys (64×128=8,192) plus decoupled values (64×128=8,192) = 16,896 dims/layer/token are cached (as the DeepSeek V2 paper's inference section states), the ratio is ≈1.94× — nowhere near 50–60×. The DeepSeek V2 paper's own claim of MQA-equivalent KV cache implies 128× reduction, also outside the stated range. The number may be correct under specific unstated assumptions (different d_c, different model variant, different caching policy), but those assumptions are not shown.
root_cause: The derivation basis — which quantities are physically cached, which model dimensions are used, and whether the comparison is at equal precision — is unspecified. The [DERIVED] label promises a derivation that this chapter does not provide and does not cross-reference.
correction: Either show the derivation inline (inputs → formula → result → sanity check) or add an explicit cross-reference to where it is derived (e.g., 'derived in Ch. 3 §X'). Specify which quantities are cached (c_KV only, or c_KV + decoupled components) and which model dimensions are used. If the number comes from a specific paper or benchmark, cite it.
acceptance_test: A reader can locate the derivation, identify the inputs and caching assumption, and reproduce a number within the stated 50–60× range — or the range is corrected to match the reproducible result.

page_hint: §6 Architecture Consequence, prefill levers paragraph
quoted_clause: Lowering precision (FP8, or BF16 in place of FP16) does not reduce the underlying algorithmic operation count (the usual 2 × params × tokens FLOPs are approximately unchanged — the matmuls still multiply the same matrices); rather it reduces the precision, lowers the bytes transferred/stored, and can raise the effective accelerator throughput (8-bit tensor cores run at higher peak rate).
observed: The sentence groups BF16-in-place-of-FP16 with FP8 as examples of 'lowering precision' whose effects include 'lowers the bytes transferred/stored' and 'can raise the effective accelerator throughput.' BF16 and FP16 are both 2 bytes per parameter; BF16 does not lower bytes vs FP16. On H100, BF16 and FP16 also share the same dense tensor-core peak (989 TFLOPS), so BF16 does not raise effective throughput on this hardware either. The sentence structure implies all listed effects apply to all listed examples.
evidence: FP16 = 2 bytes, BF16 = 2 bytes (both 16-bit formats). H100 BF16 dense = 989 TFLOPS; H100 FP16 dense = 989 TFLOPS (same peak). FP8 = 1 byte; H100 FP8 dense = 1,979 TFLOPS (2× peak). Only FP8 lowers bytes and raises peak throughput on H100. BF16 trades mantissa bits (8 vs 10) for exponent range at the same byte count.
root_cause: Two distinct precision changes (byte-count change vs mantissa-width change at same byte count) grouped under one set of claimed effects.
correction: Separate the examples: 'Lowering byte-width precision (e.g., FP8) lowers the bytes transferred/stored and can raise effective throughput (8-bit tensor cores run at higher peak rate). Changing format at the same byte width (e.g., BF16 in place of FP16) does not change bytes or peak throughput on H100 but trades mantissa bits for exponent range.' Or restrict the parenthetical example to FP8 and mention BF16 separately with its actual trade-off.
acceptance_test: No reader can infer from the sentence that BF16 reduces memory footprint or raises H100 peak throughput relative to FP16.

page_hint: Section 2, Mental Model, first paragraph
quoted_clause: the system is first-order memory‑capacity‑bound (the KV cache's HBM footprint limits how many concurrent requests fit — KV HBM capacity limits concurrency, not bandwidth — at the Ch 17 concurrency screen) and prefill‑dominated in FLOPs
observed: The sentence places 'first-order memory-capacity-bound' as a main-clause predicate, with the concurrency-screen scoping buried in a long parenthetical. A skimming reader could miss the parenthetical and read the claim as a general system characterization (true at all operating points), when it is specifically about the Ch 17 concurrency screen. At low concurrency the system is latency-bound, not memory-capacity-bound.
evidence: The parenthetical correctly scopes the claim, but the sentence structure makes both 'memory-capacity-bound' and 'prefill-dominated' appear as parallel general characterizations. Only the first is scoped; the second (prefill-dominated in FLOPs) is genuinely general for this workload.
root_cause: Scoping qualification embedded in a parenthetical rather than integrated into the main clause structure, creating asymmetric readability between the two claims.
correction: Restructure so the scoping is in the main clause: e.g., 'the system is prefill-dominated in FLOPs; at the Ch 17 concurrency screen it is also memory-capacity-bound, because the KV cache's HBM footprint limits how many concurrent requests fit (KV HBM capacity limits concurrency, not bandwidth).' This makes the generality of the FLOP claim and the specificity of the capacity claim immediately visible.
acceptance_test: A reader skimming only the main clause (ignoring parentheticals) correctly understands that memory-capacity-bound applies specifically to the concurrency screen, not to all operating points.

page_hint: Section 8, End-of-Chapter Mini-Case, final paragraph
quoted_clause: prefix-cache hit ratio ~13% and the predicted ~13% prefill reduction explain the 2.4 s → <2 s move
observed: The mini-case attributes the p95 TTFT recovery (2.4 s → <2 s) to a ~13% prefix-cache prefill reduction, but the same mini-case establishes ~18.6× prefill oversubscription at 40 rps. A 13% demand reduction leaves ~16.2× oversubscription. If service time ≈ 1.2 s and queueing at 2.4 s p95 ≈ 1.2 s, a 13% queueing reduction yields ≈ 1.04 s queueing → ≈ 2.24 s p95 TTFT, still above the 2 s SLO. The chapter itself states prefix caching is 'a partial mitigation, not the fix for the 40 rps prefill queue' (§3 Reading Telemetry, §6 Architecture Consequence), directly contradicting the mini-case's mechanism check.
evidence: Recompute: 51.6 PFLOP/s demand × 0.87 = 44.9 PFLOP/s; 44.9 / 2.77 = 16.2× still oversubscribed. Queueing component at 2.4 s p95 ≈ 2.4 − 1.2 = 1.2 s; 1.2 × 0.87 = 1.044 s; new p95 ≈ 1.2 + 1.044 = 2.244 s > 2.0 s. The stated resolution list ('additional hosts, chunked prefill, admission control/backpressure, or P/D disaggregation') is never confirmed in the mechanism check — only prefix caching is.
root_cause: The mini-case conflates two different resolutions: the capacity/scheduling measures listed as 'the resolution' and the prefix-cache mechanism check. The mechanism check confirms only prefix caching, which the chapter itself has already established as insufficient at this oversubscription level.
correction: Revise the mechanism check to confirm the actual resolution. If additional hosts were added, state the new host count and resulting capacity ratio. If chunked prefill or admission control was enabled, state the scheduling change and its expected effect on queueing. Prefix caching can be mentioned as a contributing factor (~13% prefill reduction) but must not be presented as the primary explanation for 2.4 → <2 s. Alternatively, restructure the mini-case so that the oversubscription is much lower (e.g., 1.3×) where a 13% reduction could plausibly cross the SLO boundary — but this would require changing the 40 rps / 1-host setup.
acceptance_test: After revision, recompute: (a) the stated mechanism(s) must quantitatively account for the 2.4 → <2 s improvement; (b) the mechanism check must be consistent with the resolution sentence; (c) the chapter's own claim that prefix caching is 'a partial mitigation, not the fix' must not be contradicted.

page_hint: Section 1, Concept — The Metric Hierarchy, item 2 (Serving metrics)
quoted_clause: the canonical SLO targets are TTFT 1.2 s / TPOT ~25 ms
observed: Section 1 presents 'TTFT 1.2 s' as an SLO target without a percentile qualifier. Sections 3 and 4 of the same chapter state the SLO as 'p95 ≤ 2 s' with 1.2 s as a design budget: 'We budget TTFT ≤ 1.2 s … with a p95 ≤ 2 s' (§3) and 'State the SLO window (p95 ≤ 2 s TTFT)' (§4). A reader of §1 alone would believe the TTFT SLO is 1.2 s, but the actual SLO is p95 ≤ 2 s. The 1.2 s figure is a design budget (presumably for p50 or mean), not the SLO.
evidence: §1: 'TTFT 1.2 s' labeled as 'SLO targets.' §3: 'We budget TTFT ≤ 1.2 s … with a p95 ≤ 2 s.' §4: 'State the SLO window (p95 ≤ 2 s TTFT).' Three different presentations of the same parameter within one chapter.
root_cause: The design budget (1.2 s) and the SLO (p95 ≤ 2 s) are conflated in §1. The percentile qualifier and the budget-vs-SLO distinction are missing.
correction: Revise §1 to: 'the canonical design budget is TTFT 1.2 s / TPOT ~25 ms, with an SLO of p95 TTFT ≤ 2 s' — or whatever formulation matches Ch 4 Table 4-2. Ensure the same budget-vs-SLO distinction is used consistently across the chapter.
acceptance_test: A reader of §1 alone should be able to state both the design budget and the SLO (with percentile) without contradiction when they reach §3 and §4.

page_hint: §6, Architecture Consequence, first bullet
quoted_clause: If prefill is FLOP-bound (as it is for 70B+ models with long contexts), the primary optimization is batching
observed: The opening claim 'the primary optimization is batching' is not scoped to throughput. The bullet's final sentence scopes it ('first-order throughput lever'), but a reader who stops after the first sentence concludes batching is the primary optimization for compute-bound prefill in general — including latency. The mini-case later states 'Batching helps when prefill is occupancy-limited' (not when compute-saturated), providing a different nuance for latency.
evidence: Bullet opening: 'the primary optimization is batching.' Bullet closing: 'as the first-order throughput lever.' Mini-case: 'Batching helps when prefill is occupancy-limited; kernel fusion helps when GEMMs are under-saturated.' The mini-case's nuance is not referenced from the Architecture Consequence bullet.
root_cause: The throughput scoping appears only at the end of a long bullet; the opening sentence overstates for latency-sensitive readers.
correction: Add 'for throughput' to the opening clause: 'the primary optimization for throughput is batching' — or add a forward reference: '...is batching (for latency, see the mini-case's occupancy-vs-saturation distinction).'
acceptance_test: The first sentence of the bullet does not permit a reader to conclude that batching is the primary latency optimization for compute-bound prefill.

page_hint: Section 4 (Measurement), bullet 2 and bold text immediately below
quoted_clause: Effective utilization — SLO-qualified goodput ÷ sustained SLO-qualified capacity (both measured at the same SLO) … effective utilization = SLO-meeting goodput ÷ theoretical capacity
observed: Effective utilization is defined twice within the same section with different denominators: the bullet uses 'sustained SLO-qualified capacity' (a measured capacity at the SLO) while the bold summary line uses 'theoretical capacity' (an analytical upper bound). These are not synonymous and yield different values for the same metric.
evidence: Bullet: denominator = sustained SLO-qualified capacity. Bold line: denominator = theoretical capacity. A system delivering 50% of theoretical but 90% of sustained SLO-qualified capacity would report 50% or 90% depending on which definition the reader applies. The bold line further states 'cost per useful request uses the effective definition,' making the ambiguity consequential for the chapter's headline metric.
root_cause: Two independent definitions of the same metric were written without reconciliation.
correction: Unify on one denominator. If the intent is the measured SLO-qualified capacity (which is more actionable for cost-per-request), change the bold line to 'SLO-meeting goodput ÷ sustained SLO-qualified capacity.' If the intent is the analytical bound, change the bullet accordingly. State explicitly which denominator the cost-per-useful-request calculation uses.
acceptance_test: Both definitions in Section 4 use the same denominator phrase; the cost-per-useful-request formula in the chapter references that single definition.

page_hint: Section 3, Mode 2 (cloud GPU instances), H_required equation and its definition
quoted_clause: H_\text{required} = \int_0^T N_\text{required}(t)\,dt + N_\text{warm}\cdot T_\text{warm} + R_\text{reserved} … N_\text{required}(t) is the number of hosts that must be running at time t
observed: N_required(t) is defined as 'the number of hosts that must be running at time t.' Warm-pool hosts are also running (they are warm), so a literal reading includes them in the integral, double-counting them against the separate N_warm·T_warm term. The text asserts 'every term is counted exactly once,' but the definition of N_required(t) does not support that assertion without an implicit exclusion.
evidence: If N_required(t) includes warm-pool hosts (because they 'must be running'), then ∫N_required(t)dt already contains N_warm·T_warm, and adding it again overcounts. The parenthetical '(a step function that rises with the load curve)' hints at serving-only but does not override the primary definition. Dimensional check: all three terms are host-hours, so the double-count would be silent.
root_cause: The definition of N_required(t) uses 'must be running' rather than a serving-specific qualifier, creating ambiguity with the warm-pool term.
correction: Redefine N_required(t) as 'the number of hosts required to serve the load at time t (excluding warm-pool and reserved hosts)' or equivalently 'serving hosts at time t.' Alternatively, restructure the equation so the integral covers all running hosts and remove the separate warm-pool term.
acceptance_test: The definition of N_required(t) explicitly excludes warm-pool and reserved hosts, or the equation is restructured so no term can be double-counted under any reasonable reading.

page_hint: §17.6 Architecture Consequence, Observability
quoted_clause: Alerts should trigger when per-host concurrency exceeds 80% of C, when LB error rate exceeds 0.1%, or when cross-host bandwidth utilization exceeds 70%.
observed: Three specific alert thresholds (80%, 0.1%, 70%) are presented as recommendations without [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] labels or sources.
evidence: No evidence label, citation, or scope qualifier accompanies these thresholds. Elsewhere in the chapter, similar engineering thresholds (ρ values, Gini 0.3, latency inflation 20-50%) are explicitly labeled.
root_cause: Unlabeled thresholds in a section that otherwise follows the evidence-labeling convention.
correction: Add [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] to the sentence, or provide a source/scope for each threshold.
acceptance_test: Each threshold carries an evidence label or citation.

page_hint: §18.4, Measurement, opening sentence
quoted_clause: To operate a mixed fleet we measure four cross-cutting metrics:
observed: The text says 'four cross-cutting metrics' but the table below has five rows. The fifth row is labeled '(diagnostic)' which may explain the discrepancy, but the text does not say 'four cross-cutting metrics and one diagnostic' — it says 'four' and then shows five rows.
evidence: Table rows: (1) Weighted average cost/token, (2) Per-model throughput, (3) Routing accuracy, (4) p95 of per-request service latency per model, (5) Token latency p95 per model (diagnostic). Count = 5.
root_cause: The fifth row was likely added during a review round without updating the count in the introductory sentence.

page_hint: §8 Architectural actions, SLA scoping paragraph
quoted_clause: the end-to-end request is ~9 s because of the base generation ... treats end-to-end as bounded by the ~8.6 s base generation in the incremental view (or by the full service time W ≈ 11.5 s at the median T = 1 in the fleet-sizing view)
observed: 'End-to-end' is used for three different quantities in the same paragraph: ~9 s (L_base + T·L_agent = 8.82 s subtotal), ~8.6 s (just L_base), and ~11.5 s (full service time W).
evidence: Table 19-1: Base + orchestration subtotal at T=1 = ~8.8 s; L_base = ~8.6 s; W(1) = ~11.52 s. The text uses 'end-to-end' for all three.
root_cause: The term 'end-to-end' is applied to a subtotal, a lower bound, and a full service time without distinguishing them.
correction: Use distinct terms: 'subtotal' for ~9 s, 'base generation' for ~8.6 s, and 'full service time' for ~11.5 s. Reserve 'end-to-end' for one specific quantity (preferably the full service time W).

page_hint: Ch 22, §8 mini-case, 'The peak, not the average' paragraph
quoted_clause: a homogeneous cluster sized at ~16 hosts clears both budgets
observed: The same paragraph calculates ~16.3 hosts at 40% MFU as needed for prefill at the 40 rps peak. 16 hosts × 3.164 PFLOPS/host = 50.62 PFLOPS, which is less than the 51.52 PFLOP/s required. 16 hosts would NOT clear the prefill budget; 17 hosts would (17 × 3.164 = 53.79 > 51.52).
evidence: 40 × 1.288 = 51.52 PFLOP/s needed; 7.91 × 0.4 = 3.164 PFLOPS/host; 51.52 / 3.164 = 16.28 hosts needed; 16 < 16.28 so 16 hosts fall short by ~0.9 PFLOPS.
root_cause: Rounded down from 16.3 to 16 when stating sufficiency; capacity calculations must round up.
correction: Change '~16 hosts' to '~17 hosts' (or 'at least 17 hosts') to be consistent with the ~16.3 calculation in the same paragraph.
acceptance_test: Verify that the stated host count × 3.164 PFLOPS/host ≥ 51.52 PFLOP/s.

page_hint: Ch 23 §1 Concept, first paragraph after the list intro
quoted_clause: all of it is decided by six numbers we can extract from a customer conversation
observed: The chapter's central framing claims six 'numbers,' but in the worked example (§3) only three of the six bounds are numeric: traffic (~10/40 rps), token profile (~9,200/~300), and latency (TTFT ≤ 2 s, ~25 ms/token). Bound 4 is a test design (50-question benchmark, not a quality threshold), Bound 5 is qualitative ('on-prem, regulated'), and Bound 6 is qualitative ('within a self-host budget'). §6 then calls them 'six bounds,' introducing a second term for the same set.
evidence: Dialogue §3: Bound 4 = 'a 50-question retrieval-QA quality benchmark' (test size, not accuracy target); Bound 5 = 'the regulated-data constraint makes the local/server tier the preferred path'; Bound 6 = 'within a self-host budget.' None of these is a number in the sense the concept section promises. §6 says 'six bounds,' not 'six numbers.'
root_cause: The concept section over-promises quantification; the dialogue honestly produces a mix of numeric and qualitative constraints, but the framing sentence was not updated to match.
correction: Either (a) reframe as 'six constraints' or 'six bounds' throughout (concept section, §4 'all six numbers,' §6 'six bounds'), or (b) show how to quantify Bounds 4–6 in the dialogue (e.g., '≥90% accuracy on the 50-question set,' 'data must not leave premises,' '$X/month ceiling'). Option (b) would strengthen the chapter's own thesis.
acceptance_test: Search Ch 23 for 'six numbers'; every occurrence should match the actual content of the six bounds, or the framing should be changed to 'six bounds/constraints.'

page_hint: Ch 24 §6, item 2 (RAG corpus policy)
quoted_clause: a 64 B tag over ~48,000 chunks is ~3 MB, well under 1% of the corpus
observed: The claim 'well under 1%' depends on what 'the corpus' means, and no basis is specified. If the corpus is the FAISS vector index: 48,000 × 768-dim × 4 B (FP32) ≈ 147 MB → 3/147 ≈ 2 %; at FP16 ≈ 74 MB → 3/74 ≈ 4 %. If 1,536-dim FP32 ≈ 295 MB → 3/295 ≈ 1 % (borderline). If the corpus is raw document text (12,500 docs × 10–50 KB ≈ 125–625 MB), 3 MB is 0.5–2.4 %. The claim is unsupported without a specified denominator.
evidence: 3 MB / (48,000 × 768 × 4 B) = 3/147 ≈ 2.0 %. 3 MB / (48,000 × 768 × 2 B) = 3/74 ≈ 4.1 %. Neither is 'well under 1%.' The text does hedge with 'the real overhead depends on the provenance encoding and must be measured,' but the specific 'well under 1%' claim is made before that hedge.
root_cause: The denominator ('the corpus') is ambiguous — vector index vs. raw text vs. something else — and the embedding dimension/precision is not stated.
correction: Specify the denominator: e.g., 'well under 1% of the raw document text (12,500 documents ≈ X MB)' or 'well under 1% of the vector index (48,000 × D-dim × P-byte ≈ Y MB).' If the intended denominator is the raw text, state the assumed document size.
acceptance_test: The claim 'well under 1%' can be verified by multiplying the stated tag size by the stated corpus size and confirming the ratio.

page_hint: Ch 23 §8, 'The burst buffer, spelled out' paragraph
quoted_clause: an idealized 100% MFU ceiling (≤141 rps — 7B FP16, ~500 output tokens/request, H100), i.e. ~42–57 rps at 30–40% MFU
observed: The 141 rps figure is the decode-only rate (based on 500 output tokens). For this workload (500 input + 500 output), prefill and decode have equal FLOPs (2NL × 500 each = 7 TFLOP each), so including prefill roughly halves the total request-completion rate: ~71 rps at 100 % MFU, ~21–28 rps at 30–40 % MFU. The worked example then uses r = 50 rps (decode-only at ~35 % MFU), but the actual total service rate at 35 % MFU including prefill is ~25 rps. This makes the burst-drain numbers (150 queued, 3 s drain) optimistic by ~2×. The text does say 'the measured per-host rate must replace this,' but never notes that prefill competition is a specific reason the actual rate would be lower.
evidence: One H100 at 100 % MFU: 989 TFLOPS. Decode-only: 989e12 / 14e9 = 70,643 tok/s → 70,643/500 = 141 rps. Total (prefill + decode): 989e12 / (14e12) = 70.6 rps. At 35 % MFU: decode-only ≈ 49 rps, total ≈ 25 rps. Worked example uses r = 50 (decode-only). With r = 25: queue = 175, drain = 7 s, total from burst start = 8 s (vs. text's 150 / 3 s / 4 s).
root_cause: The 141 rps ceiling is computed from output tokens only (decode), but the text presents it as the service rate r without noting that prefill for the same 500 input tokens consumes an equal share of compute.
correction: Add an explicit note: 'This is the decode-only ceiling; for this workload (500 in / 500 out) prefill and decode have equal FLOPs, so the total request-completion rate including prefill is roughly half — ~71 rps at 100 % MFU, ~21–28 rps at 30–40 % MFU. The worked example below uses r = 50 (decode-only) as an optimistic illustration; the measured rate must replace it.' Alternatively, recompute the worked example with r ≈ 25 and note it as the total rate.
acceptance_test: The text explicitly states whether r is decode-only or includes prefill, and the worked-example numbers are consistent with that choice.

page_hint: Ch 23 §8, mirror restatement sentence
quoted_clause: a 7B-class model on one on-prem GPU, resolving baseline tickets under 3 s, with a 200-rps burst buffer
observed: The mirror restatement — which the chapter frames as the scope-locking moment — does not mention the degraded-mode SLO for burst traffic. The subsequent burst-buffer analysis (same section) concludes that burst-window requests miss the 3 s SLO and need 'a separate queue-and-drain degraded-mode SLO.' This is a significant scope decision that the restatement omits.
evidence: Mirror restatement lists: model, GPU, 3 s SLO, burst buffer, quality gate, pilot. Burst analysis concludes: 'burst-window requests miss the 3 s SLO, so the burst runs under a separate queue-and-drain degraded-mode SLO (option a).' The final paragraph acknowledges 'the 3 s SLO scoped to non-burst traffic, the burst served under the queue-and-drain degraded mode' — but this appears after the restatement, not in it.
root_cause: The restatement was written before the burst analysis revealed the need for SLO scoping; it was not updated afterward.
correction: Add to the mirror restatement: '…with a 200-rps burst buffer served under a degraded queue-and-drain SLO (separate from the 3 s baseline).' This makes the restatement complete and consistent with the analysis that follows.
acceptance_test: The mirror restatement includes every scope decision that the subsequent analysis in the same section establishes as necessary.

page_hint: §25.7 What We Still Don't Know, item 4
quoted_clause: [1P][FACT] — no widely adopted tool exists for ADR graph visualization or impact analysis (a factual tooling observation, not an open hypothesis).
observed: The claim "no widely adopted tool exists" is tagged [1P][FACT], but it is a negative claim about the tooling landscape that is difficult to verify exhaustively. [1P][FACT] implies first-party factual knowledge, which is hard to establish for a claim about the absence of tools.
evidence: The author cannot survey every tool in existence. The claim is reasonable but its strength exceeds what [1P][FACT] typically signals in this book's taxonomy (e.g., hardware specifications, format bit-widths).
root_cause: Overly strong evidence tag for a negative claim about tool existence.
correction: Either downgrade to [1P][DERIVED] (derived from the author's knowledge of the landscape) or scope the claim with a date (e.g., "no widely adopted tool was identified as of [date]").
acceptance_test: The evidence tag matches the verifiability of the claim; a negative existence claim does not carry [FACT] without exhaustive survey evidence.

page_hint: Ch 8 §6 Architecture Consequence, third bullet, final sentence
quoted_clause: This is why the H200 represents an inflection point where inference and training hardware lines begin to converge [1P: NVIDIA H200 SXM datasheet].
observed: The claim that H200 is an 'inflection point where inference and training hardware lines begin to converge' is a strong editorial interpretation not supported by the cited datasheet, which documents specifications, not market-positioning or architectural-convergence claims. H200 is H100 with more/faster HBM3e; it is not a new architecture.
evidence: The datasheet cited is a specifications document. The 'inflection point' framing is the author's interpretation, not a first-party claim. The preceding arithmetic (lower ridge due to more bandwidth at similar compute) is correct, but it does not establish an industry-level 'inflection point'.
root_cause: Editorial overreach: a defensible local observation (H200's ridge is lower than H100's) is inflated into a broad industry claim.
correction: Either remove the 'inflection point' sentence or reframe it as a scoped observation: 'H200's lower ridge means some workloads that are memory-bound on H100 become compute-bound on H200 — a reminder that the ridge is a hardware property, not a workload property.' If the convergence claim is retained, cite a source that actually makes it.
acceptance_test: The sentence either is removed or is supported by a source that explicitly makes the convergence claim; the local arithmetic observation is preserved without the unsupported industry framing.

page_hint: Ch 8 §3, 'Scope note on the single-device roofline here' paragraph
quoted_clause: each GPU streams only its own shard (~0.70 TB/s against its own ~3.35 TB/s, Ch 6)
observed: The phrase '~0.70 TB/s against its own ~3.35 TB/s' is cryptic: it is unclear whether 0.70 TB/s is a demand, a rate, or a comparison. The intended meaning (per-GPU weight-stream demand vs. per-GPU HBM bandwidth) requires the reader to reconstruct the arithmetic.
evidence: 140 GB / 8 GPUs = 17.5 GB per GPU per token; at ~25 ms TPOT, demand ≈ 0.70 TB/s. The text does not show this derivation.
root_cause: Compression of a two-step derivation into a parenthetical.
correction: Expand to: 'each GPU streams only its own ~17.5 GB shard, demanding ~0.70 TB/s of its ~3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth at the canonical TPOT — well within the per-GPU ceiling'.
acceptance_test: A reader can see what 0.70 TB/s represents (per-GPU demand) and why it is compared to 3.35 TB/s (per-GPU capacity) without reconstructing the arithmetic.

page_hint: Chapter 15, Table 15-1 (Light row) and §5 Common Mistakes
quoted_clause: kernel regime (§3) ... Compute (SDPA)
observed: Table 15-1 labels the Light row's kernel regime as 'Compute (SDPA)' at the canonical 9,500-token context. §5 Common Mistakes says: 'For long contexts (9,200+ tokens) the O(L²) intermediate makes the naive kernel memory-traffic-bound.' These are contradictory descriptions of the same SDPA kernel at the same context length.
evidence: The table's own note says the kernel regime is 'a kernel property — it does not change across these three load regimes'. If the SDPA kernel is memory-traffic-bound at 9,200+ tokens per §5, it cannot be 'Compute' in the Light row at 9,500 tokens. The contradiction is internal to the chapter and affects the roofline diagnosis the table is meant to teach.
root_cause: The table conflates the aggregate prefill compute demand (a workload-level capacity signal) with the attention kernel's roofline regime (a kernel-level property). The Light row's 'Compute (SDPA)' appears to be a leftover from an earlier framing in which prefill was treated as uniformly compute-bound.
correction: Make the kernel-regime label consistent with §5.
